title: Courage 4 Zongchi
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up the story of Bodhidharma's four disciples and the nun Zongchi, drawing on Andy Ferguson's Zen's Chinese Heritage, Dogen's "Katto" chapter of the Shobogenzo, and Sallie Tisdale's Women of the Way. Heigaku opens with last week's koan of the old woman and Hakuen, then reads Bodhidharma's "skin, flesh, bones, marrow" exchange, where Dogen insists the four answers are not ranked. Tisdale imagines Zongchi walking with Bodhidharma beside the Great Wall, free of her palace life. Heigaku then explores Akshobhya Buddha through his association with water, and reads Zongchi's line, "felt at the first glance, but not at the second," as a caution against grasping any arising experience.

sentences.text: So we studied the koan of the old woman with Hakuen, who was studying his words regarding looking into her heart to see light, pondering them day and night.
When she was just doing everyday work, she had a great insight that she took to him, enjoying and seeing it everywhere.
He challenged her steadfastness with some crass language, and she responded with joy.

We observed that there was that push from him and a push back from her, and maybe he was checking to make sure she was still human, still aware of her everyday nature, of her everyday body, that that doesn't go away after the experience.
In several of our services, we dedicate the merit of our practice with the lines, we dedicate this merit to our first ancestor in China, great teacher Bodhidharma.
Bodhidharma was a monk who traveled from India to China to teach Buddhism, in his words, to rescue the deluded by transmitting the Dharma.
Bodhidharma had four disciples, the most famous of whom is Hwike.
Another of his disciples is the nun called Zongchi, or Soji in Japanese.
Several sources observed that the restrictions on the interactions of monks and nuns and nuns were very strong at this time, which is the fifth century of the common era.
So it isn't certain how he was able to get away with flouting those rules by having a woman as part of the gang.
Grace Shearson notes that research from Shasta Abbey suggests Bodhidharma's own teacher in India, Prajnatara, was a woman, which may have predisposed him to clarity on the issue.
The only teaching that we have from Zongchi is the statement of her understanding that she gave to Bodhidharma when he cut his students loose in preparation for returning to India.
One translation of the traditional story is from *Zen's Chinese Heritage* by Andy Ferguson on page 16.
After nine years, Bodhidharma wanted to return to India.
Calling together his disciples, he said, "The time for me to return to India is at hand.
Can each of you say something to demonstrate your understanding?"
A disciple named Daofu said, "As I see it, it is not bound by words and phrases, nor is it separate from words and phrases.
This is the function of Dao."
Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my skin."
The nun Zongchi said, "According to my understanding, it is like a glorious glimpse of the realm of Akshobya Buddha.
Seen once, it need not be seen again."
Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my flesh."
A disciple named Daoyu said, "The four elements are all empty and the five skandhas are without actual existence.
As I see it, there is not a single Dharma to be grasped."
Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my bones."
Thereupon, Hwike bowed and stood up straight.
Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my marrow."
In the Kato chapter of *Shobogenzo*, Eihei Dogen analyzes this traditional story, and I am quoting Reverend Hubert Neerman's translation.
Dogen writes, "What you need to explore through your training is that our first Chinese ancestor's statement, you have realized my skin, flesh, bones, and marrow, is what the ancestor said.
Each of his four disciples respectively expressed what they had realized.
Each demonstrated what they had learned.
What they all had realized is the skin and flesh, bones and marrow, which sprang forth from their own body and mind.
It is the skin and flesh, bones and marrow of dropping off body and mind.
This is beyond anything that someone can gather from an ancestral master by means of intellectual understanding based on observation, which is simply comparable to one move in a game of Go."
Likewise, it is not something that fully manifests before one's eyes as subject and object, or as this and that.

At the same time, folks who have not experienced the genuine transmission fancy that there were relative degrees of intimacy in what each of the four disciples comprehended, so that what the ancestor was saying was that skin, flesh, bones, and marrow are not the same in their profundity.

They think that skin and flesh are coarser than bones and marrow, and they say that the discerning thought of the second ancestor had surpassed that of the others, so that he alone obtained the certification of knowing what the marrow was.
Those who talk like this have still not explored through their training what the Buddhas and ancestors are, nor have they experienced the genuine transmission of what the ancestors speak.
Dogen is saying that each of their understandings was a component of receiving Bodhidharma's body, a whole body without one greater than another.
In the book *Women of the Way*, Sallie Tisdale does tremendous research into histories such as this one, and fills in the story herself, providing a realistic picture of what life was like.
Her account of this event is on page 116, or 133 of the e-book.
She writes, "Bodhidharma had no fear in him.
So this is Zongqi's experience.
Bodhidharma had no fear in him, no interest in, or patience with intrigue and status.
He didn't care about convention at all.
He perhaps did not know that Zongqi was the emperor's daughter, but if he had known, he would not have cared.
Zongqi never asked to stay, conscious of the rules that said monks were not allowed to consort with women.
Conscious too, almost against her will, of all she had absorbed about the Confucian order of high and low, which placed women forever below men.
In the Buddhist world, people said that men and women were equal in enlightenment.
But that didn't mean equal in the world."
Men and women didn't mix like this, didn't live together, and could be punished for it.
If Bodhidharma had told her to leave, she would have gone.
But he didn't, so she stayed.
The three monks with whom she traveled merely made room for her in the small circle.
If the monks at the temples where they stopped for a few nights' shelter complained to the muscular Indian about bringing a woman into their midst, she never heard about it.
Perhaps no one dared complain to the monk who had turned his back on an emperor and lived.
She took on their poor and simple life, wearing rough clothes, eating plain vegetables and a little grain, rising early every day.

They never stayed in one place for long, but walked through the city streets and sometimes out into the suburbs, among the poorest of the poor, the rural peasants who had found their way full of hope to the city.

Zongqi spent long, long days sitting with Bodhidharma in front of any nearby wall, the walls of city streets, the walls of cliffs and caves, slit walls and rock walls, walls of trees and walls of people.
One year they walked north and went to gaze on the great wall, being built block by block, for a mile on endless mile.
They watched the thousands of drafted men, covered in sweat and sorrow, building the wall into the misty hills, and then they sat beside it for a while.
The mind, he liked to say, should be like a wall.
When the way is clear, then the way is clear.
They didn't talk much, but lived closely, depending on each other.
Huike, with his one arm, had been Bodhidharma's student since they met in Shaolin.
He was jovial where his teacher was stern.
Daofu liked to chatter, and Dayu saved his breath for philosophy.
They were companions and became friends.
Zongqi had grown up inside, inside the court, inside a palace, inside a world and a role.
Now she was outside, outside her rank and status and even sometimes her gender.
Instead of small rooms and screens and curtains, now her world was bordered by fields and storm clouds and steep mountain paths.
She had grown up with precise instructions as to her place and purpose in life, and now she found herself with no purpose but her own.
"To find a Buddha, all you have to do is see your own nature," said Bodhidharma.
And around her she seemed to see her nature in rocks and trees, stationary, stolid, alive.
"Your nature is the Buddha," he continued, "and the Buddha is the person who is free, free of plans, free of cares."
And she was.
She became a person without boundaries.
She ceased to think in terms of in and out, high and low.
She ceased to think of the edges of herself and the edges of the world as being different things.
One day, without formality or warning, Bodhidharma gathered them together and asked for a summary of what they had learned.
"What have I given you?" he said in his blunt way.
Daofu stepped forward immediately.
"I have come to see that Buddhism is not about words, but we have to discuss it in words."
Bodhidharma said, "Yes, this is my skin."
Then Zongqi stood before her teacher, close enough to smell the sweat on his robe.
Joyfully, she said, smiling, joyfully, "I understand that knowing the way is like seeing paradise.
Once is enough."
"Yes," he said, "this is my flesh."
It was Daoyu's turn, and he let go of philosophy.
"The elements truly have no essence.
The aggregates don't even exist.
I cannot attain a thing."
"Yes, this is the bone."
Finally Huike, who is the oldest of them, saw step forward and simply bowed, slowly and deeply, and then stood aside in silence.
Bodhidharma said, "Yes, this you know is the marrow."
Skin, flesh, bone and marrow.
A body.
His body.
His teacher's body.
His teacher's teacher's body before him, and back and back through time and space.
A Buddha body needing all these things to live.
The skin of form, the flesh of action, and the bones and marrow of heart and mind.
A whole body, nothing extra, nothing missing.
Zongqi and the others wore the same robes and carried the same kind of bowl, and each was unique.
Each had received something else.
Something there is alone, invisible to others, and very precious.
Combining half a dozen different translations, here is Zongqi's statement about practice realization that seems most complete to me.
"It is like Ananda's glorious joy upon seeing the land of the Buddha Akshobhya.
It is felt at the first glance, but not at the second glance."
For some background, Akshobhya Buddha is known as the Immovable One, Lord of the Eastern Pure Land, Abhirati.
Akshobhya Buddha is colored blue from transforming the energy of greed, hate and delusion into wisdom.
The story is that a monk made a vow to think no anger or malice toward any being until enlightenment, and that is how that monk became Akshobhya Buddha.

I had to go to Wikipedia to learn about Akshobhya Buddha, which is ironic because a few months ago a Zen teacher of mine from the East whom I rarely see, advised me to study Akshobhya, but I hadn't gotten to it yet.

I believe the lesson being referred to by Kotatsu Roko is the association of Akshobhya Buddha with the element water, summarized in Wikipedia as follows: *Even if the surface of the ocean is blown into crashing waves, the depths remain undisturbed, imperturbable.
And though water may seem ethereal and weightless, in truth it is extremely heavy.
Water flows into the lowest places and settles there.
It carves through solid rock, but calmly, without violence.
When frozen, it is hard, sharp and clear, like the intellect.
But to reach its full potential, it must also be fluid and adaptable, like a flowing river.
These are all the essential qualities of Akshobhya.*
Akshobhya is also known as the embodiment of mirror knowledge, where the mind itself discern reality from illusion.
This is consistent with Zangchi's teacher's focus on direct experience of Buddha nature.
I don't know what circumstances of Ananda's visit to the Eastern Pure Land are, but certainly the mode of travel was clear insight into the nature of reality.
We know Ananda as one of Shakyamuni Buddha's principal disciples.

He is credited with being the one best able to remember all of the Buddha's teachings, but he didn't understand them as well as the others, not attaining enlightenment until after Shakyamuni Buddha's death.
We also met Ananda a few weeks ago in this class.
He is the one who intervened on behalf of Mahapajapati and convinced Shakyamuni Buddha to permit women to ordain.
While the first half of Zangchi's statement is a reference to the heavenly joy of practice realization, the crux of the koan seems to be in the second half.
"It is felt at the first glance, but not at the second glance."
To me that refers to the experience of joy or pain or any other skandha arising.
We are truly present with it in the arising, and with the transient changing nature of all phenomena, if we try to grasp it, to get a second glance, we are creating suffering.
Our effort on the cushion is carried into the everyday of our lives.

Having the courage to meet what is truly present, not what we assume is present based on our memories and beliefs, but what presents itself now, that is the light-hearted engagement we are capable of.
What is it to live life aware and unchained from ourself?
It is like Ananda's glorious joy upon seeing the land of the Buddha Akshobhya.
It is felt at the first glance, but not at the second glance.
